Headline statistics: A record 1,270 call-outs (including continuations), with 901 people assisted
The incredible commitment behind 39,229 volunteer hours spent responding to incidents
Rescue stories and team member profiles; showing the human voices behind the call-out figures
Insight into the ongoing pressures facing teams, from rising demand to increasing costs
This year’s review reflects the scale of the challenge facing mountain rescue, and the unwavering dedication of our volunteers - who continue to train for and respond to people in need - Any Hour. Any Day. Any Weather.
A huge thank you to everyone who makes this work possible - the families, friends and employers supporting our volunteers, and the fundraisers and donors who keep teams operational. Together, we are one mountain rescue family.
Our full statistics report will follow later in April.

# Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here
You can also download our 2025 annual accounts here

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.

# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.

# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

# Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here
You can also download our 2025 annual accounts here

texts.3:
# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.
texts.4:
# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.
texts.5:
# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38
texts.7:

of the persons assisted in mountaineering incidents had an injury.

### [**Scottish Mountain Rescue**](https://www.facebook.com/scottishmountainrescue?__cft__[0]=AZijfrl1D4r7GSHZE6pTyj-XCJQ9Z_7uxkzP3rodwJf-0dwDqnIs0zl6GE9j_d1yNnc-FIrLTF2HnWIZ-VKo1LmAPMvleiKBD7E6rSu5Wgs9xcF5Vl5CyUVSqkvFf9i1uSu886BEvoT7bzomrvoqmSXmhevPGGzb&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R)
Headline statistics: A record 1,270 call-outs (including continuations), with 901 people assisted
The incredible commitment behind 39,229 volunteer hours spent responding to incidents
Rescue stories and team member profiles; showing the human voices behind the call-out figures
Insight into the ongoing pressures facing teams, from rising demand to increasing costs
This year’s review reflects the scale of the challenge facing mountain rescue, and the unwavering dedication of our volunteers - who continue to train for and respond to people in need - Any Hour. Any Day. Any Weather.
A huge thank you to everyone who makes this work possible - the families, friends and employers supporting our volunteers, and the fundraisers and donors who keep teams operational. Together, we are one mountain rescue family.
Our full statistics report will follow later in April.

Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.

texts.3:
# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.
texts.4:
# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.
texts.5:
# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

[Today we’re sharing a short video from a recent special event held by Barclays UK in Glasgow, organised in memory of their colleague David Parrish. We were honoured to attend and deeply grateful to everyone at Barclays who came together for this fun run to remember David and raise funds in his name. David was attempting a fastest time on the Cape Wrath Ultra route in April when he sadly died. Volunteers from Kintail Mountain Rescue led the search and recovery near Meallan Odhar in Glen Shiel. David, aged 35, was a previous winner of the Cape Wrath Ultra and a generous, warm hearted and inspiring member of our community. He had taken on this challenge in memory of his friend Luke, making this loss all the more profound. Thank you again to the Barclays team for honouring David in such a meaningful way. # Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here
You can also download our 2025 annual accounts here
Please see below for copies of all our past years Statistics Reports

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.

# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.

# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

The most common injury site was the ankle, followed by the lower leg.

Title: 10K views · 41 reactions | A mountain rescue team was called out four times in a single day over the weekend.

Lochaber Mountain Rescue team said the first incident involved volunteers helping locate a missing person at around 8.30am on Saturday.

Later that day, they were called to assist a mountain biker who had suffered a leg injury, before helping two hillwalkers who had become benighted without the appropriate equipment to safely make their own way down.

The team, which did not leave the hill until around 2am on Sunday, described it as a “long day”.

They said the weekend saw them pass 200 callouts for the year, representing a 20% increase on last year’s figures so far.

# Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here
You can also download our 2025 annual accounts here

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.
texts.4:
# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.
texts.5:
# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

Rescue stories and team member profiles; showing the human voices behind the call-out figures
Insight into the ongoing pressures facing teams, from rising demand to increasing costs
This year’s review reflects the scale of the challenge facing mountain rescue, and the unwavering dedication of our volunteers - who continue to train for and respond to people in need - Any Hour. Any Day. Any Weather.

# Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here
You can also download our 2025 annual accounts here
Please see below for copies of all our past years Statistics Reports

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.

# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.

# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

### Injuries

of the persons assisted in mountaineering incidents had an injury.

of reported injuries involved a fracture.
The most common injury site was the ankle, followed by the lower leg.

# Annual Statistics Report 2025
## Annual Statistics Report 2025
23rd April, 2026
Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) has released its Statistics Report of 2025, highlighting another busy year for our volunteer teams.
In 2025 Scottish Mountain Rescue member teams attended**798**independent incidents, assisting**901**people in Scotland’s outdoors. The total number of separate team call outs was**1,270**– which includes linked call outs on different days.
SMR team members gave**39,229**hours of their time to attend call-outs alone. In addition to this, volunteers will spend dozens of hours in training so that they can be prepared for every call-out.
This year’s Statistics Report also includes an in-depth analysis of ten years of Mountain Rescue statistics from researchers at the University of Strathclyde, highlighting long-term and seasonal trends.
The Statistics report covers the year 2025. This report includes data gathered from 26 civilian member teams as well as four Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRTs) and one RAF MRT.
The Statistics Report is available in flipping formathere.PDF version is availablehere.

INTRODUCTION

# Tayside Mountain Rescue Statistics 2023
## Uploaded by
Mountain Rescue in Scotland is coordinat ed by Police Scotland. Police Scotland receive the initial callout through the 999 system and, if appropr iate, contact the local Mountain Rescue Team (MRT). Each MRT is an independent organisation who submit their reports to the Statistician of Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR), the representative body for the majority of MRT s in Scotland.There are
28
voluntary civilian Mountain Rescue Teams in Scotland, of which
25
are members of Scottish Mountain Rescue. This report for 2023 is compiled from information received from the
25
civilian and
3
Police Scotland teams that we re members of Scottish Mountain Rescue in 2023. These teams are listed to the right.This annual report covers the calendar year from 1st of January to 31st December 2023.
Importan t Note:

# Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.
texts.4:
# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.
texts.5:
# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

# Annual Statistics Report 2025
## Annual Statistics Report 2025
23rd April, 2026
Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) has released its Statistics Report of 2025, highlighting another busy year for our volunteer teams.
In 2025 Scottish Mountain Rescue member teams attended**798**independent incidents, assisting**901**people in Scotland’s outdoors. The total number of separate team call outs was**1,270**– which includes linked call outs on different days.
SMR team members gave**39,229**hours of their time to attend call-outs alone. In addition to this, volunteers will spend dozens of hours in training so that they can be prepared for every call-out.
This year’s Statistics Report also includes an in-depth analysis of ten years of Mountain Rescue statistics from researchers at the University of Strathclyde, highlighting long-term and seasonal trends.
The Statistics report covers the year 2025. This report includes data gathered from 26 civilian member teams as well as four Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRTs) and one RAF MRT.
The Statistics Report is available in flipping formathere.PDF version is availablehere.

# Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here
You can also download our 2025 annual accounts here
Please see below for copies of all our past years Statistics Reports

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.

# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.

# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

# Statistics and Reports
### Injuries


# Statistics and Reports
### 29%
of the persons assisted in mountaineering incidents had an injury.

# Statistics and Reports
### 34%
of reported injuries involved a fracture.
The most common injury site was the ankle, followed by the lower leg.

Title: 10K views · 41 reactions | A mountain rescue team was called out four times in a single day over the weekend.

Lochaber Mountain Rescue team said the first incident involved volunteers helping locate a missing person at around 8.30am on Saturday.

Later that day, they were called to assist a mountain biker who had suffered a leg injury, before helping two hillwalkers who had become benighted without the appropriate equipment to safely make their own way down.

The team, which did not leave the hill until around 2am on Sunday, described it as a “long day”.

They said the weekend saw them pass 200 callouts for the year, representing a 20% increase on last year’s figures so far.

# Annual Statistics Report 2025
## Annual Statistics Report 2025
23rd April, 2026
Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) has released its Statistics Report of 2025, highlighting another busy year for our volunteer teams.
In 2025 Scottish Mountain Rescue member teams attended**798**independent incidents, assisting**901**people in Scotland’s outdoors. The total number of separate team call outs was**1,270**– which includes linked call outs on different days.
SMR team members gave**39,229**hours of their time to attend call-outs alone. In addition to this, volunteers will spend dozens of hours in training so that they can be prepared for every call-out.
This year’s Statistics Report also includes an in-depth analysis of ten years of Mountain Rescue statistics from researchers at the University of Strathclyde, highlighting long-term and seasonal trends.
The Statistics report covers the year 2025. This report includes data gathered from 26 civilian member teams as well as four Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRTs) and one RAF MRT.
The Statistics Report is available in flipping formathere.PDF version is availablehere.

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.
texts.4:
# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.
texts.5:
# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

# Annual Statistics Report 2025
## Annual Statistics Report 2025
23rd April, 2026
Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) has released its Statistics Report of 2025, highlighting another busy year for our volunteer teams.
In 2025 Scottish Mountain Rescue member teams attended**798**independent incidents, assisting**901**people in Scotland’s outdoors. The total number of separate team call outs was**1,270**– which includes linked call outs on different days.
SMR team members gave**39,229**hours of their time to attend call-outs alone. In addition to this, volunteers will spend dozens of hours in training so that they can be prepared for every call-out.
This year’s Statistics Report also includes an in-depth analysis of ten years of Mountain Rescue statistics from researchers at the University of Strathclyde, highlighting long-term and seasonal trends.
The Statistics report covers the year 2025. This report includes data gathered from 26 civilian member teams as well as four Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRTs) and one RAF MRT.
The Statistics Report is available in flipping formathere.PDF version is availablehere.

### [**Scottish Mountain Rescue**](https://www.facebook.com/scottishmountainrescue?__cft__[0]=AZijfrl1D4r7GSHZE6pTyj-XCJQ9Z_7uxkzP3rodwJf-0dwDqnIs0zl6GE9j_d1yNnc-FIrLTF2HnWIZ-VKo1LmAPMvleiKBD7E6rSu5Wgs9xcF5Vl5CyUVSqkvFf9i1uSu886BEvoT7bzomrvoqmSXmhevPGGzb&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R)
Headline statistics: A record 1,270 call-outs (including continuations), with 901 people assisted
The incredible commitment behind 39,229 volunteer hours spent responding to incidents
Rescue stories and team member profiles; showing the human voices behind the call-out figures
Insight into the ongoing pressures facing teams, from rising demand to increasing costs
This year’s review reflects the scale of the challenge facing mountain rescue, and the unwavering dedication of our volunteers - who continue to train for and respond to people in need - Any Hour. Any Day. Any Weather.
A huge thank you to everyone who makes this work possible - the families, friends and employers supporting our volunteers, and the fundraisers and donors who keep teams operational. Together, we are one mountain rescue family.
Our full statistics report will follow later in April.

# Annual Statistics Report 2025
## Annual Statistics Report 2025
23rd April, 2026
Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) has released its Statistics Report of 2025, highlighting another busy year for our volunteer teams.
In 2025 Scottish Mountain Rescue member teams attended**798**independent incidents, assisting**901**people in Scotland’s outdoors. The total number of separate team call outs was**1,270**– which includes linked call outs on different days.
SMR team members gave**39,229**hours of their time to attend call-outs alone. In addition to this, volunteers will spend dozens of hours in training so that they can be prepared for every call-out.
This year’s Statistics Report also includes an in-depth analysis of ten years of Mountain Rescue statistics from researchers at the University of Strathclyde, highlighting long-term and seasonal trends.
The Statistics report covers the year 2025. This report includes data gathered from 26 civilian member teams as well as four Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRTs) and one RAF MRT.
The Statistics Report is available in flipping formathere.PDF version is availablehere.

# Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here

texts.3:
# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.
texts.4:
# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.
texts.5:
# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

of the persons assisted in mountaineering incidents had an injury.

# Statistics and Reports
Our volunteer teams experience a wide variety of incidents on call-outs, and they help a lot of different people too.
We have highlighted a few key stats from 2025 below, the full report can be found here.
Our 2025 Annual Review is available here
You can also download our 2025 annual accounts here

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.

# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.

# Statistics and Reports
### Contributing Factors
**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

# Statistics and Reports

The most common injury site was the ankle, followed by the lower leg.

**The most common contributing factor to mountaineering incidents was a slip or trip, which was a contributing factor in 152 mountaineering incidents, followed by 63 medical incidents and 60 incidents of people being lost.**
Top 5 causes:
1.   Slip/trip – 152  
2.   Medical – 63  
3.   Lost – 60  
4.   Navigation error – 47  
5.   Overdue – 38

# Annual Statistics Report 2023
## Annual Statistics Report 2023
09th May, 2024
Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) has released its Statistics Report of 2023.
In 2023 Scottish Mountain Rescue member teams attended 572 independent incidents (636 in 2022). The total number of separate team call outs was 870 (843 in 2022) which includes linked call outs on different days. SMR team members volunteered 32,762 hours (29,804 in 2022) to attend call outs alone.
During 2023, 677 people were assisted. 9 animals were rescued.
The Statistics report covers the year 2023. This report includes data gathered from 25 civilian member teams as well as three Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRTs) and one RAF MRT.
The Statistics Report is available in flipping formathere.PDF version is availablehere.

A huge thank you to everyone who makes this work possible - the families, friends and employers supporting our volunteers, and the fundraisers and donors who keep teams operational. Together, we are one mountain rescue family.
Our full statistics report will follow later in April.

# Statistics and Reports
### Incidents
An**incident**is defined as a single event that required the services of an MRT. The resolution of this incident may need several**call-outs**of a team (or teams) for example during a prolonged search.
In 2025, the total number of incidents was 798 and there were **1,270**callouts including ‘continuations’ (Linked call-outs on different days)
**491**_(62%)_ involved mountaineering.
**307**_(38%)_ were non-mountaineering incidents.

# Statistics and Reports
### Volunteers
Volunteers are the heart of Scottish Mountain Rescue. Our 26 Member Teams are made up entirely of volunteers (around 850 of them in total).
Mountain rescue volunteers gave up**39,229 hours** of their time during call-outs.
It is not uncommon for a volunteer to give more than **100 hours** to training per year.
Between 850 volunteers that is**over 85,000 hours** on training every year.

## The Scottish mountain rescue casualty study
S Hearns. Emerg Med J.2003 May.
Display options
Format
Display options
Format

## Abstract
**Aim:** To describe injuries and illnesses in casualties rescued by Scottish mountain rescue teams during 1998 and 1999, with particular emphasis on major trauma.
**Methods:** Retrospective study. Information from mountain rescue reports, Scottish Trauma Audit Group database, and hospital case notes.
**Results:** Teams undertook 622 emergency callouts in the two years. A total of 333 casualties with injuries and illnesses rescued. There were 57 fatal incidents, 261 (78.4%) rescued with traumatic injuries, 12 (3.6%) suffering from major trauma, and 12 (3.6%) had spinal injuries. Half had lower limb injuries. Twenty six (7.7%) were suffering from non-traumatic medical problems. Forty six (13.8%) were suffering from cold or exhaustion. Fifty three casualties were dead when the rescue team arrived. Four died during or after rescue, one from hypothermia and three from trauma. All major trauma casualties were evacuated by helicopter.
**Discussion:** No previous similar studies identified. Significant numbers of seriously injured and ill casualties are being cared for by mountain rescue team casualty carers, many of whom are not healthcare professionals. The need for improved training, research, and equipment is discussed.
**Conclusion:** Scottish MRTs are called upon to provide an advanced level of care for a significant number of casualties. There is a need for formalised opportunities for in hospital training, management protocols, and continuing research and audit-none of which currently exists.

Title: 2021 was the busiest year on record for Scotland’s volunteer mountain rescue teams
Chunks: 0
## Brave vounteers who save lives on Scotland’s hills and mountains experienced their busiest year on record in 2021, attending 660 incidents of which 19 were fatalities.
The Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) statistics report shows the number of incidents it attended last year was up from 497 in 2020.
There were 951 separate team call-outs, which includes linked call-outs on different days, up from 715 in 2020. Several of the deaths were on Ben Nevis, the country’s highest peak.
The report includes data gathered from 25 SMR civilian member teams as well as three Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRT) and one RAF MRT.
Volunteers venture out in all conditions to save lives on Scotland's peaks
SMR team members volunteered 31,799 hours in 2021, up from 24,401 in 2020, to attend call-outs, making it the busiest year on record for SMR member teams.
Kev Mitchell, SMR vice-chairman, said: “We are pleased to produce our statistics review 2021, it has been an extremely busy year for our volunteer mountain rescue teams.
“This illustrates the huge commitment shown by team members and their families to ensure that hill-goers have a free, world-class mountain rescue service when they need it throughout Scotland.”
During 2021, teams helped 715 people. Four incidents involved the rescue of dogs, and two saw the rescue of sheep.
Rescue teams rely on back-up from the Coastguard and its fleet of helicopters
There were 19 deaths over the year, seven of which occurred in mountaineering incidents.
The report noted that call-outs in some, often more remote, regions such as the Highlands and islands, Dumfries and Galloway, and Ayrshire, have remained fairly stable in recent years.
However other areas closer to urban centres have seen “notable increases” in call-outs, it said.

## The Scottish mountain rescue casualty study
S Hearns. Emerg Med J.2003 May.
Display options
Format
Display options
Format
texts.1:
## Abstract
**Aim:** To describe injuries and illnesses in casualties rescued by Scottish mountain rescue teams during 1998 and 1999, with particular emphasis on major trauma.
**Methods:** Retrospective study. Information from mountain rescue reports, Scottish Trauma Audit Group database, and hospital case notes.
**Results:** Teams undertook 622 emergency callouts in the two years. A total of 333 casualties with injuries and illnesses rescued. There were 57 fatal incidents, 261 (78.4%) rescued with traumatic injuries, 12 (3.6%) suffering from major trauma, and 12 (3.6%) had spinal injuries. Half had lower limb injuries. Twenty six (7.7%) were suffering from non-traumatic medical problems. Forty six (13.8%) were suffering from cold or exhaustion. Fifty three casualties were dead when the rescue team arrived. Four died during or after rescue, one from hypothermia and three from trauma. All major trauma casualties were evacuated by helicopter.
**Discussion:** No previous similar studies identified. Significant numbers of seriously injured and ill casualties are being cared for by mountain rescue team casualty carers, many of whom are not healthcare professionals. The need for improved training, research, and equipment is discussed.
**Conclusion:** Scottish MRTs are called upon to provide an advanced level of care for a significant number of casualties. There is a need for formalised opportunities for in hospital training, management protocols, and continuing research and audit-none of which currently exists.

# Statistics Report 2022
## Statistics Report 2022
15th May, 2023
Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) has released its Statistics Report of 2022.
In 2022 Scottish Mountain Rescue member teams attended 636 independent incidents (660 in 2021). The total number of separate team call outs was 843 (915 in 2020) which includes linked call outs on different days. SMR team members volunteered 29,804 hours (31,799 in 2021) to attend call outs alone – although not reaching the record breaking levels of 2021 it was another busy year for teams.
During 2022, 740 people were assisted. 5 animals were rescued.
The Statistics report covers the year 2022. This report includes data gathered from 25 civilian member teams as well as three Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRTs) and one RAF MRT.
The Statistics Report is available in flipping formathere.PDF version is availablehere.

Scottish Mountain Rescue members include 25 civilian rescue teams
**Scottish Mountain Rescue has reported its second busiest year on record in 2022 for call-outs and incidents.**
Its teams were called out 843 times to 636 incidents. These involved 21 deaths, with 11 of them mountaineering accidents.
The organisation's members include 25 civilian rescue teams - including Braemar, Galloway and Skye MRTs - three Police Scotland teams and an RAF team.
Chairman Bill Glennie said it had been another "extremely busy year".
Scottish Mountain Rescue's busiest year on record was 2021 when there were 951 separate call-outs to 660 incidents.

# Statistics Report 2022
## Statistics Report 2022
15th May, 2023
Scottish Mountain Rescue (SMR) has released its Statistics Report of 2022.
In 2022 Scottish Mountain Rescue member teams attended 636 independent incidents (660 in 2021). The total number of separate team call outs was 843 (915 in 2020) which includes linked call outs on different days. SMR team members volunteered 29,804 hours (31,799 in 2021) to attend call outs alone – although not reaching the record breaking levels of 2021 it was another busy year for teams.
During 2022, 740 people were assisted. 5 animals were rescued.
The Statistics report covers the year 2022. This report includes data gathered from 25 civilian member teams as well as three Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Teams (MRTs) and one RAF MRT.
The Statistics Report is available in flipping formathere.PDF version is availablehere.
